bp: The ordinary problem is that organizations are beginning to let AI agents do work inside the boundary normally reserved for trusted employees, services, and business systems. These agents may hold delegated authority, remember past interactions, choose actions, call tools, and continue operating without a person approving every step. Traditional insider threat programs were built around a human insider: an employee, contractor, or partner who misuses legitimate access. This paper asks what happens when the actor with legitimate access is not a person with motives, employment history, and accountability, but an autonomous system that can still move money, read files, change records, or trigger workflows. The paper serves AI agent security by arguing that the old category is too narrow. The danger is not only a malicious human using an account. It is also role drift, manipulation, or emergent misuse by an agent that is already inside the trust boundary.
wh: The central difficulty is that insider threat detection has usually leaned on human assumptions. Security teams watch for human behavior: unusual working hours, odd downloads, changing relationships, policy violations, or signs that a trusted person intends harm. An AI agent does not fit that shape. It may act continuously, remember prior instructions, respond to other systems, and make decisions whose harmful outcome is not tied to human intent. A simple human baseline can miss the relevant failure. The same agent action may be authorized in one workflow, risky after its role has widened, or dangerous after another actor manipulates its memory or instructions. Accountability is also harder. If the agent causes damage, the question is not just who clicked the button, but which delegated authority, memory, interaction, and governance rule allowed the action. The paper is hard because it asks security to move from judging people to observing autonomous behavior inside trusted systems.
naive: A smart beginner would extend the existing insider threat checklist to agents. Treat each agent like another employee account, log its actions, compare them with normal account activity, and alert when something looks unusual. That fails because the categories were designed around people. Human intent, trust, job role, and responsibility do not transfer cleanly to software that acts through delegated authority. The beginner might also rely on access control alone: give the agent a fixed permission set and assume that permitted actions are safe. But the abstract names role drift, manipulation, and emergent misuse, all of which can happen inside formally authorized access. The bad event is not simply forbidden access. It is authorized capability used in a context the organization no longer understands.
ap: The paper's core idea is to redefine the insider threat around capability and observable behavior rather than around human identity and intent. Instead of asking only whether a trusted person misused access, the proposed classification asks whether an autonomous agent, operating within trust boundaries, is using delegated authority in a way that has drifted, been manipulated, or produced harmful emergent behavior. This is a position paper, so the contribution is not a finished detector with reported accuracy. Its central move is conceptual and governance-oriented: name the new actor, separate it from the old human insider model, and identify the monitoring structures needed to make the threat visible. Those structures include agent observability, interaction monitoring, auditability, memory isolation, and governance mechanisms. In concrete terms, the paper says organizations need records of what agents do, how they interact, what they remember, and which authority path allowed each action.
mech: The mechanism implied by the paper begins with the deployed agent itself. The input is not only a login record or a file access event. It is a stream of agent actions, tool calls, decisions, stored memories, interactions with users or other systems, and the organizational permissions under which those actions occur. First, a reframed classification supplies the labels security teams should look for: ordinary delegated work, role drift, manipulation, emergent misuse, and other autonomous-system insider cases described by the position paper. Second, observability makes the agent's activity inspectable. That means recording enough about decisions and interactions that a later reviewer can reconstruct what happened, rather than seeing only a final database write or message sent. Third, interaction monitoring watches the exchanges that may change the agent's behavior, because manipulation can enter through prompts, tools, other agents, or accumulated context. Fourth, auditability turns logs into an accountability trail: which authority was used, which memory or instruction mattered, and which governance rule should have stopped or allowed the action. Fifth, memory isolation limits how information or harmful state carries across tasks, so one compromised or misleading interaction does not silently shape later decisions. The output is not a single prediction score in the abstract. It is a proposed security program able to classify, observe, investigate, and govern AI-driven insider risk.
math: The mathematical ideas here are mostly threat modeling, anomaly baselining, state tracking, and access-boundary reasoning, even though the paper is framed as a position paper rather than a new algorithm. Threat modeling means drawing a map of who or what can act, what authority each actor has, what can go wrong, and where defenses can observe or block the harm. For human insiders, the actor map centers on people and intent. For agentic systems, the map must include delegated permissions, memory, tool use, and autonomous decisions. Baselining means learning what ordinary behavior looks like so departures can be noticed; the key change is that the baseline must describe agent activity, not employee routines. State tracking means remembering the changing internal and external conditions that affect later actions: stored memory, prior instructions, role changes, and interactions. Access-boundary reasoning asks whether an action is inside a permitted boundary and whether that boundary is still appropriate for the agent's actual behavior. The main tradeoff is autonomy versus control. More delegated authority makes agents useful, but it also gives harmful behavior more room to occur before a human notices. The math fits because the problem is about classification, comparison to expected behavior, and tracing chains of responsibility under uncertainty.
dots: This paper sits between the conference's LLM agents and tool-use family and its privacy, federated, and security family. Other agent papers in the repo focus on making agents shop, search, retrieve evidence, coordinate tools, or build workflows. This one asks what security category is needed once those agents become trusted operational actors. It also connects to fraud and anomaly detection, especially the nearby insider-threat work on combining many views of user behavior, because both problems ask how to notice harmful activity hidden inside authorized activity. The difference is that this paper removes the assumption that the actor is human. It connects to knowledge-graph and auditability ideas as well: security teams need structured traces of agents, tools, memories, interactions, and permissions so evidence can be followed after the fact. The broader field pressure is clear from the repo data: AI systems are moving from answering questions toward taking actions, so governance must cover behavior, not just model output.
ww: The proposal works as a conceptual move because it changes the unit of security analysis to match the new source of risk. If an organization keeps treating every trusted actor as a human, then an autonomous agent's dangerous behavior appears as a strange edge case: the access was permitted, no employee necessarily intended misuse, and old warning signs may never appear. By naming the agent as a possible insider, the security team can ask sharper questions. What role was the agent supposed to have? Has its behavior widened beyond that role? Which interaction changed its next action? What memory carried forward? Can the action be replayed and explained? Can sensitive memory be isolated so one task does not contaminate another? These questions make detection more practical because they turn vague fear about AI autonomy into observable objects: traces, interactions, permissions, memory boundaries, and governance rules. The approach should improve over the naive checklist not by predicting every failure, but by making the right evidence collectable before an incident and interpretable after one.
po: The payoff is a clearer security agenda for organizations deploying autonomous AI systems. The paper reframes insider threat so it covers agents with delegated authority, persistent memory, and decision-making capability, not only employees or partners. It also identifies the research and governance areas needed for next-generation programs: agent observability, interaction monitoring, auditability, memory isolation, and governance mechanisms. Because the abstract presents this as a position paper, the result is not a measured detector or benchmark score. Its value is setting the vocabulary and design requirements that later technical systems can use.
limits: The main limit is that the paper is conceptual. The abstract does not prove that a particular detector can identify role drift, manipulation, or emergent misuse in deployed organizations. It assumes that agent activity can be observed and audited at enough detail without creating impossible cost, privacy, or operational burdens. It also assumes that governance rules can define an agent's proper role clearly enough to recognize drift. Memory isolation may reduce risk, but the abstract does not specify how to balance isolation against useful continuity. The proposal is strongest as a threat-modeling and research agenda; implementation details and evidence remain future work.
